check: internal code names, database field names or enum values showing in the UI (`snake_case`, `camelCase`, ALLCAPS_ENUM in visible text).

text: Write an abbreviation out in full at its first use on a page and use the short form after that; only well-known ones (BBC, NHS, UK) or ones search data shows people know may skip this. WCAG 3.1.4 (AAA) needs a way to reach the expansion, such as the full form right before or after first use; `<abbr>` by itself is only advisory.
check: regex `\b[A-Z]{2,}\b` per screen, then confirm each has an expansion earlier on the same page.

text: For cognitive-disability audiences, drop or explain uncommon acronyms, abbreviations and jargon; for global audiences, keep to common abbreviations (USB) or those in a glossary.
check: acronyms from TEXT-31 that are neither expanded nor in the product's glossary, on screens serving these audiences.

text: Keep one word per level of obligation: "must" (not "shall") for requirements, and "must not", "may", "should" for the rest.
check: grep `\bshall\b` in terms, policies and settings help.

text: Capitalise sentence-style in headings, titles and UI labels (first word and proper nouns only); no all caps for emphasis or for long text; no capitals inside words unless a brand has them.
check: Title Case Headings in locale strings; `text-transform: uppercase` on body text.

text: For non-native readers and machine translation (global products, more than one locale), apply this rule and TEXT-36 to TEXT-40. Start by cutting idioms, colloquialisms and references that only one culture gets (sports, holidays, local history).
check: read for them; grep a short idiom list.

text: Keep the normal subject-verb-object order and keep the "that", "who" and articles that help translation.
check: telegraphic strings whose meaning is unclear (a label such as "Access denied" can read better as "Access is denied").

text: Break up modifier stacks (long runs of nouns and adjectives in front of a noun).
check: 4+ nouns or adjectives in a row before the head noun.

text: Join no more than three phrases or clauses with and/or/but, and preferably no more than two.
check: count coordinating conjunctions per sentence.

text: Use few sentence fragments, and make the role of -ing and -ed words clear with a determiner or a form of "be".
check: verbless fragments in body text; ambiguous -ed/-ing phrases such as "added functionality" with no article.

text: Talk about months or quarters rather than seasons; if a season must appear, say which hemisphere.
check: grep -i `(spring|summer|autumn|fall|winter) (release|sale|update)`.

text: Keep wording gender-neutral: "you", singular "they", role names (reader, customer); no "he/she" or "s/he" for a generic person; neutral nouns (chair, staff, workforce).
check: grep -iw `he|she|his|her|he/she|s/he|chairman|manpower|mankind|salesman`.

text: Put the person before the disability (people who are blind, not "the blind"), leave out words that signal pity ("suffering from", "stricken with"), and mention a disability only when it matters.
check: grep -i `suffer|stricken|wheelchair-bound|handicapped`.

text: Replace terms carrying racial, military or historical baggage: primary/subordinate for master/slave, perimeter network for DMZ, "stop responding" for "hang".
check: grep -iw `master|slave|whitelist|blacklist|kill|abort|hang` in UI strings.

text: In examples, vary names and roles, pick places that are not disputed, avoid generalising about people or regions, and avoid slang or appropriated phrases ("spirit animal").
check: sample data, placeholder names, onboarding personas.

text: Write numbers in digits ("23", and 2 to 9 too); add a comma above 999 ("9,000"); write ranges as "500 to 900" rather than "500-900" outside tables. The sources disagree on a number that opens a sentence: GOV.UK writes it out, NN/g keeps digits.
check: grep spelled-out numbers `\b(two|three|four|five|six|seven|eight|nine|ten)\b` near units.

text: Write large numbers as digits plus a magnitude word ("24 billion", "138 billion" with the currency symbol); explain trillions for most readers and billions for less numerate or international ones. COGA asks for alternatives to numbers and numerical ideas.
check: raw figures longer than 7 digits in the UI; percentages or rates given to a public audience with no plain comparison.

text: State exact figures when they are known; use words only for amounts that are not specific facts ("thousands of").
check: vague quantities ("many", "a number of", "lots of") where the product holds the real count.

text: Give dates with the month as a word and without ordinals: "4 June 2017" (GOV.UK) or "January 5, 2018" (Microsoft); never all-digit dates like 05/01/2018 for an international audience; "to" rather than a dash in date and time ranges; "on or before" for deadlines.
check: grep `\d{1,2}/\d{1,2}/\d{2,4}` and `toLocaleDateString()` with no explicit month format.

text: Make times easy to read: "5:30pm" rather than "1730hrs", "midday"/"midnight" rather than "12pm"/"00:00", "11:59pm" for a cut-off; add the time zone when it matters (events, deadlines) unless the time is already shown in the reader's local time.
check: deadlines with no time zone in a product used across regions.

text: Money: use the currency symbol and show ".00" only when there are pence or cents (GOV.UK: 75.50 is fine, 75.00 is not); pair "%" with a number.
check: grep `\.00\b` in rendered prices.

text: Hold one voice across the product and shift tone to match the reader's emotional state and the subject; Mailchimp frames voice as constant and tone as changing.
check: compare onboarding, billing, error and email copy for a voice that changes between them.

text: Leave humour out where readers are frustrated or see the message repeatedly (errors, retries, failures), since NN/g found it can annoy; Mailchimp's default when in doubt is to stay serious. Error-message content and blame: see web.md.
check: jokes, puns or emoji on error, payment, data-loss or security screens.

text: Stay away from the extremes of NN/g's four tone dimensions (formal-casual, serious-funny, respectful-irreverent, matter-of-fact-enthusiastic), and suit tone to the brand and domain (a bank's error message should not be playful).
check: exclamation marks and slang in finance, health or legal flows.

text: For public health or risk messages, use the CDC Clear Communication Index (20 scored items, among them one main message placed at the top, active voice, common numbers, number meaning, behavioural recommendation); OADC recommends a score of 90 or more out of 100, agreed by two reviewers.
check: a health or risk page without one main message at the top or without a clear action for the reader; score it on the Index sheet.

text: Delete means the thing is gone from the system (perhaps to a trash first); "Remove" means it leaves this list, view or collection but still exists. Pair them the way people expect — Create with Delete, Add with Remove — and use the same verb for one action on the button, the menu, the confirmation and the toast that follows.
check: grep the labels and copy; a "Remove" that destroys data, a "Delete" that only hides it, or one action named differently in two places.

text: Everything a mouse can do, the keyboard can do too, right-click menus included; build clickable pictures and boxes from real button controls.
check: run each core task with no mouse; grep for click handlers on elements that cannot take focus (`PointerPressed` on `Image`, `onClick` on `div`).

text: Leave the well-known shortcuts meaning what users expect: Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+Y redo, Ctrl+X/C/V, Ctrl+A, Ctrl+F, F3 next result, F2 rename, F5 refresh, Ctrl+S, Ctrl+W close, Ctrl+P, Ctrl+N, Ctrl++/Ctrl+-/Ctrl+0 zoom; macOS uses the Command versions plus Shift-Command-Z redo and Command-Comma settings.
check: try each key in the app; grep keydown handlers that call `preventDefault` on one of these and do something else.

text: Stay off the modifiers the OS owns: Super in GNOME apps, Alt+letter on Windows/GNOME (access keys live there), and Control on macOS.
check: grep accelerator strings for `Super`, `Meta`, `Alt+<letter>`, and mac-only `Ctrl+`.

text: Spend custom shortcuts only on the commands people repeat most; build them from Ctrl/Command plus a letter, use an added Shift for the inverse or extended form of a related shortcut, and never reuse an existing combo plus a modifier for something unrelated.
check: compare the custom shortcut list; flag Shift+Ctrl+Z (or Shift-Cmd-Z) mapped to anything other than redo.

text: Electron accelerators use `CommandOrControl`, so a single binding becomes Cmd on macOS and Ctrl on Windows and Linux.
check: grep `accelerator:` for a bare `Ctrl+`/`Command+` with no platform branch.

text: Teach shortcuts in the places people look: next to the item in main menus and inside the button tooltip (custom tooltip text must still carry it), but leave them off context menus.
check: hover or focus toolbar buttons that have shortcuts; open the menus; grep `ToolTipService.ToolTip` on controls with `KeyboardAccelerators`.

text: F6 moves focus to the next major pane (sidebar, toolbar, content) and Shift+F6 to the previous one; in WinUI the app has to build this itself.
check: from launch, press F6 again and again; focus should land in every major region and come back round.

text: Esc backs out of anything temporary (menu, popover, dialog, an open combo box, which reverts to its earlier value) and out of a pointer action under way such as a drag; it never closes or navigates back in the main window.
check: open each temporary surface, start a drag, then press Esc.

text: Tab order runs top to bottom and left to right (mirrored per locale), each label comes just before its control, and only things you can operate get a stop.
check: the Tab stops step of Accessibility Insights FastPass; grep for positive `TabIndex`/`tabindex`.

text: A cluster of related controls (list, grid, radio group, toolbar) takes one Tab stop; arrows move inside it and Home/End jump to its ends; in native Windows controls, wrapping from last to first is for popup menus only. Web ARIA widgets follow their APG pattern instead, where tabs do wrap (A11Y-63).
check: Tab into a list — one stop, arrows move within, the next Tab leaves; judge wrapping by the native-or-web split above.

text: When a window or page opens, focus sits on the action people most likely want first and never on something destructive (such as Delete while reading mail).
check: open each window and page and record the focused element before typing anything.

text: Each labelled control and menu item gets an Alt access key that no sibling in the same scope shares: prefer the first letter, then a strong consonant, vowels last; skip look-alikes such as I/l/1 and O/0; no more than two characters; translated with the label.
check: tap Alt (Windows/GNOME) and read the keytips or underlines; look for repeats within one scope.

text: Keep the platform focus indicator, including on restyled controls (WinUI default: 2px primary outer border plus 1px secondary inner border); WCAG focus rules are in a11y.md.
check: grep `UseSystemFocusVisuals="False"` and `outline: none`/`outline: 0` with nothing put in their place; Tab through and screenshot.

text: macOS menu-bar order and the Window menu: IOS-57 owns the rule, for Electron and Tauri apps on macOS too.
check: IOS-57's Check.

text: Menu-bar menus list the same items every time, greying out what cannot run now rather than removing it; an item that asks for more input before it acts ends in an ellipsis.
check: open each menu with and without a selection and diff the items; look for "Save As" or "Export" lacking "...".

text: In Electron, standard items are declared with their `role` (`undo`, `redo`, `cut`, `copy`, `paste`, `selectAll`, `editMenu`, `windowMenu`, `appMenu`...) rather than hand-written click handlers, because roles give native behavior. Calling `Menu.setApplicationMenu(null)` removes the default menu, and on Windows/Linux the menu bar with it.
check: grep `label: 'Copy'` and similar without `role`; after `setApplicationMenu(null)`, confirm Cmd/Ctrl+C/V/Z/A still work in text fields.

text: A context menu holds only what applies to the thing clicked, in roughly three groups or fewer, with no submenu inside a submenu; items that cannot run are left out (Cut/Copy/Paste may stay, greyed). GNOME sizes: 3-12 items per menu, 3-6 per submenu.
check: right-click every object type; count items, groups and nesting depth.

text: Nothing lives only in a context menu: each of its commands can also be reached from the menu bar, a toolbar or a command bar.
check: for every context-menu entry, locate the same command somewhere else.

text: Every kind of object answers right-click and the Menu key / Shift+F10 on the focused item with a context menu; a right-click lists options and does not itself carry out an action such as deleting.
check: right-click and Shift+F10 on each list, row, canvas object and text field.

text: Primary windows can be resized; their first-launch size fits the content without being maximized or close to it, and growing the window reveals more content rather than more empty space.
check: launch with a clean profile and screenshot the default size; enlarge to full screen and compare.

text: Below the size where content stops working, the window refuses to shrink, and before that point the layout adapts instead of cutting things off; the Windows guide aims for an 800×600 effective minimum (a Windows 7-era guide).
check: Electron `win.setMinimumSize()`, WinUI/Win32 minimum size; drag the window as small as it goes and screenshot clipped controls.

text: On relaunch, each window comes back on the same monitor with the same size, position and maximized state; if that monitor is missing, the window is moved fully onto one that exists.
check: move and resize, quit, relaunch; repeat with the second display disconnected.

text: Closing one primary window leaves the others alone; a secondary window has a parent, is modal to it, does not open further secondary windows on top of itself and is not bigger than its parent; Ctrl+W shuts a window and Esc shuts a modal one.
check: open two documents and close one; open a dialog from inside a dialog.

text: A window the user asked for may grab input focus only if it appears within 5 seconds; a window the program opened on its own flashes the taskbar button rather than jumping to the front.
check: type in another app while a slow window opens and while a background event fires; note any focus theft.

text: On Windows, the app declares Per-Monitor V2 DPI awareness and redoes its layout when the DPI changes, sizing itself to the rectangle that `WM_DPICHANGED` proposes; apps that are unaware or only system-aware get bitmap-stretched and look blurry.
check: manifest `dpiAwareness` set to `PerMonitorV2`; grep `GetSystemMetrics(` (the per-DPI form is `GetSystemMetricsForDpi`) and fixed pixel sizes.

text: Try the app at 100%, 125% and 150% scaling, while dragging it across displays with different DPI, and while the scale is changed under a running app.
check: screenshot at every scale; look for clipped text and blurry or stretched icons.

text: Use the platform's own title bar and window buttons where possible; a home-made one that misses any of the system's look or behavior makes the whole app seem broken.
check: Electron `titleBarStyle`/`frame: false`, Tauri `decorations: false`; hold it against the next two rules.

text: A custom Windows title bar is 32px high (48px when it holds a search box or person picture); its empty areas move the window, right-click there opens the system window menu, double-click maximizes or restores, the caption buttons never get squeezed out, its elements turn semi-transparent while the window is inactive, and it recolors for light/dark and contrast themes.
check: drag, right-click and double-click empty title-bar space; make the window narrow; click into another app.

text: Inside an Electron drag region, every button and input carries `app-region: no-drag` (the region otherwise eats their clicks), text cannot be selected, no custom context menu is attached, and on Windows/Linux the window buttons are brought back (`titleBarOverlay`).
check: grep `app-region: drag`, then click each control inside it.

text: Hover is never the only way to find an action or an important piece of information (WEB-57 owns the rule); on desktop the miss is mouse users who never park the pointer there.
check: screenshot with the pointer parked away; list what appears only on hover and find another route to each.

text: Icon-only buttons in toolbars and header bars all carry a tooltip; once one control in a group has one, its neighbours do too. Tooltips on keyboard focus: WEB-12.
check: hover and then Tab along the toolbar.

text: Tooltip content follows WEB-11; desktop sources add that a tooltip never holds errors, status or anything to click, and on a disabled control it says what would enable it.
check: read every tooltip; grep tooltips that contain links or buttons or repeat their button's text.

text: Whatever can be done by dragging can also be done another way (Cut/Paste, a "Move to..." command); WCAG 2.5.7 is covered in a11y.md.
check: for each draggable item, perform the same move using only keyboard and menus.

text: Draggable things look draggable and the drop says what it will do (copy, move or link); inside one container the default is move, between containers or apps it is copy, and a drop can be undone.
check: drag between panes and into another app; press Ctrl/Cmd+Z right after dropping.

text: Modifier keys behave as on the platform: Ctrl/Cmd+click adds or removes one item, Shift+click selects a range, Shift during a resize locks the aspect ratio, arrow keys nudge what is selected, Ctrl+scroll wheel zooms.
check: try each on lists and on canvases.

text: Lists and tables allow extended selection with Ctrl+click, Shift+click, Shift+Arrow and Ctrl+A.
check: pick rows 1 and 3, then 5-9, using modifiers; then Ctrl+A.

text: With nothing selected, bulk commands are unavailable apart from Select All; clicking outside does not end selection mode; destructive bulk commands ask first.
check: open the bulk toolbar with none, one and several selected; click empty space.

text: Numbers right-aligned: VIS-43 owns that; dense tables also line up decimal points, left-align text columns, align each header with its column, and centre no column.
check: screenshot the table; inspect `text-align` on numeric `td`/`th`.

text: Users can choose row density, and the header row matches the body row size. Pencil & Paper: condensed 40px, regular 48px, relaxed 56px; Carbon: 24/32/40 (default)/48/64px. The choice survives a reload and can be reset to default.
check: measure a row; switch density, reload, confirm it stayed.

text: Pinned headers: VIS-44 owns the rule; in a wide desktop table that means the first, identifying column during horizontal scrolling too, and a totals footer may stay in view as well.
check: scroll a long, wide table in both directions; screenshot.

text: Columns can be sorted and show which state they are in (unsorted, ascending, descending) without knocking the header out of alignment; the starting sort fits the data, such as newest first or most urgent first.
check: click the headers; check `aria-sort` and the icon.

text: Every row has a checkbox and the header has a select-all checkbox that can be checked, unchecked or indeterminate; bulk actions appear only after at least one row is selected.
check: tick one row; the header checkbox should turn indeterminate and the action bar should show.

text: Row actions are visible or one evident click away (a "View more" link or a "..." menu on the row); NN/g reports that actions tucked behind hover or a generic Actions menu are hard to find.
check: screenshot with no hover; can a row action be located?

text: Editable cells show it (a text cursor on hover), a row in edit mode looks different from the rest, an edit is committed by Enter, clicking away, a checkmark or Save, and data with high stakes is edited in a modal or side panel instead of in the cell.
check: put a cell in edit mode and press Esc; (disposable only, or local scratch data) commit edits with Enter and by clicking elsewhere.

text: A long column title wraps onto two lines and is then cut off, with the whole title in a tooltip; when row heights differ by more than 3 lines, cell content sits at the top.
check: narrow the columns; hover a cut-off header.

text: Tables people use to look up or compare records are paged, with the page controls under the table; endless scrolling fits only a constant stream of flat content.
check: scroll to the end of a large table; is there a page number to come back to?

text: Columns can be hidden and reordered easily without needing drag-and-drop, the table shows that some are hidden, and an obvious reset restores the default set.
check: hide a column, reload, look for the hidden-column indicator and the reset.

text: Undo and redo go back through every action since the document was opened or saved, sit first in the Edit menu (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y; Command-Z / Shift-Command-Z), name the action they will reverse ("Undo Typing"), and scroll the affected change into view.
check: (disposable only, or a local scratch document) make 20 assorted edits, scroll away, undo all of them; read the Edit menu labels.

text: Undo before confirmation: WEB-7 owns the rule and WEB-68 the safeguard for each size of loss, on desktop as on the web.
check: (disposable only, or a local scratch document) delete something; note whether there is undo, a prompt, or neither. Read-only: read the delete handler.

text: Work is saved without being asked: at intervals during editing, on closing the file and on switching to another app.
check: (disposable only, or a local scratch document) edit, kill the process, relaunch; see what is missing.

text: A "Save changes?" prompt appears only when the user really changed something, and its buttons name the outcome (Save / Don't save) instead of OK/Cancel.
check: open and close an unedited document (expect no prompt); (disposable only, or a local scratch document) edit and close (expect one); read the buttons.

text: A dialog's confirming button says exactly what it does, Esc cancels, Return never defaults to a destructive button, and dialogs open only because the user did something and are modal to a parent window.
check: open each dialog; press Return and Esc; watch for dialogs that pop up on their own.

text: Changing a setting takes effect at once, with no OK/Save step; settings open as IOS-58 describes on macOS, and from the foot of the navigation pane (or the overflow menu) on Windows.
check: change a setting, look for an immediate effect and change it back ((disposable only) for settings stored in the user's account); press Cmd+, on macOS.

text: The settings list is short with defaults that work for most people, holds no everyday workflow commands, and shows a setting that does not apply as disabled with a reason rather than removing it.
check: count the settings; look for routine commands reachable only from settings.

text: The app follows OS-wide preferences rather than offering its own copy of them; on Windows a theme picker offers Light, Dark and "Use system setting" (the platform split: VIS-36).
check: change the OS appearance while the app runs; inspect the theme picker's options and default.

text: OS notifications are for events worth knowing about while the user is in another app; while the app is in front, new information shows up inside it (toast, badge, new row). One event gives one notification, outdated ones (already read elsewhere) are withdrawn, and users can turn the volume down or off.
check: (disposable only) fire events with the app in front and behind, twice each; read the item in the app, then look in Notification Center. Read-only: read the notification code for one-per-event, withdrawal and in-app display.

text: Clicking a notification opens the app on that item; a background action such as quick reply does its work without opening the app; a notification has three buttons at most; the app window carries everything the notification said.
check: click a notification; (disposable only) then each of its buttons that acts (reply, delete, mark done).

topic: Updates, first run and native feel
text: Updates download quietly, the user is told when one is ready and offered Restart / Later, and a failed update is reported rather than swallowed.
check: Electron `autoUpdater` / `update-electron-app` setup; grep for an `error` handler.

topic: Updates, first run and native feel
text: The app tracks the OS light/dark choice: Electron `nativeTheme.themeSource` stays `'system'`, CSS uses `prefers-color-scheme`, and a change arriving through `nativeTheme`'s `updated` event applies without a restart.
check: grep for `themeSource = 'light'`/`'dark'` set at startup; switch the OS theme while the app runs.

topic: Updates, first run and native feel
text: Contrast themes are respected: read `nativeTheme.shouldUseHighContrastColors` / `inForcedColorsMode`, draw with system colors, fix no colors under HighContrast, and try all four Windows contrast themes (Aquatic, Desert, Dusk, Night sky). Reduced motion: VIS-35.
check: toggle with Left Alt + Left Shift + Print Screen and screenshot each screen.

text: Doherty Threshold (Doherty & Thadani, IBM Systems Journal 1982): aim for a visible reaction to every user action within 400 ms; work that runs longer shows a progress indicator or other perceived-speed cue, since even an imprecise bar makes waiting easier to bear. The pass/fail lines are WEB-1's.
check: time click/keypress to first visible change on a slow network (SKILL.md: Slow network), from video frames on any platform (web: DevTools Performance, INP), and judge it by WEB-1; quote 400 ms as the target missed.

text: Fitts's Law (Paul Fitts, 1954): frequently used targets are big, spaced apart, and near where the hand or cursor already rests; the primary button sits right after the field that precedes it; with a mouse, screen edges and corners act as targets of unlimited depth (this gain disappears on touchscreens).
check: measure target box and distance from the preceding interaction (e.g. submit button far from last form field, menu options opened in a bottom sheet far from their label, tiny adjacent targets causing mis-taps). Sizes: see touch.md.

text: Tesler's Law, conservation of complexity (Larry Tesler, Xerox PARC mid-1980s; interview in Dan Saffer, *Designing for Interaction*): the product absorbs the complexity no design can remove — anything it already knows or can work out, it fills in instead of asking.
check: list every input the user must supply; any value the system could infer (city from postcode, card type from number, timezone, previously entered data) that it asks for again breaks it.

text: Hick's Law (Hick & Hyman, 1952): where speed counts, the screen offers few options, marks a suggested one, breaks big tasks into stages and reveals features gradually to newcomers — while still giving enough context that options stay meaningful.
check: count options on time-critical screens (primary nav, dialogs, checkout); a long flat list with no default/recommended option, or a first-run screen exposing every feature, breaks it.

text: Choice Overload (term from Alvin Toffler, *Future Shock*, 1970): large option sets come with ways to narrow them early (search, filters, a featured pick) and, where options must be weighed, a side-by-side comparison such as a plan table.
check: large catalogues or plan pages without filter/search/compare, or plan tiers whose differences must be read in separate pages or modals.

text: Miller's Law (George A. Miller, 1956): content is split into small, digestible groups; the seven-item figure is no justification for arbitrary caps such as limiting a menu to 7 entries, and memory span differs between people and situations.
check: flag findings or code comments that treat seven plus-or-minus two as a hard cap; treat as a smell any long ungrouped sequence the user must hold in mind (codes, steps, options).

text: Chunking (term from Miller's 1956 paper "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two"): content falls into clearly separated, ranked groups so a reader can skim straight to the part they need; long strings are displayed and entered in short segments.
check: walls of text without headings or grouping; phone/IBAN/licence keys/OTPs shown or entered as one unbroken string.

text: Cognitive Load (John Sweller, "Cognitive Load Theory, Learning Difficulty, and Instructional Design", 1988): the screen spends the user's attention only on the task; anything that demands thought without aiding understanding is removed.
check: decorative or distracting elements competing with the task area (auto-playing media, redundant banners, duplicate links), and tasks that require remembering information from a previous screen instead of showing it.

text: Serial Position Effect (term coined by Hermann Ebbinghaus; primacy and recency): the items people most need sit at the start and end of a list or nav bar; the middle holds what matters least.
check: the most-used or most important nav item or option buried mid-list while low-value items take the first/last slots.

text: Von Restorff Effect, isolation effect (Hedwig von Restorff, 1933): the one thing that matters most on a screen stands out, and only it — sparing emphasis keeps highlights from fighting each other or being mistaken for ads; the difference never rests on colour alone, and motion used for emphasis respects motion sensitivity.
check: primary-button count per VIS-22; primary action indistinguishable from secondary; emphasis carried only by hue (colour rules: see visual.md and a11y.md).

text: Zeigarnik Effect (Bluma Zeigarnik, 1920s): unfinished work stays on people's minds, so the product shows plainly that more content exists and how much of an open task remains, giving users a reason to return and finish.
check: content cut off with no visible cue that more exists (no partial item, arrow or "more"); incomplete profiles/setups/drafts with no visible remaining-steps indicator.

topic: Motivation and memory of the experience
text: Goal-Gradient Effect (Clark Hull, 1932; Hull 1934 rat-alley experiment): people speed up as the finish nears, so multi-step tasks show where the user stands and how far is left; the source adds that even artificial progress toward the goal raises motivation.
check: multi-step flows (checkout, onboarding, long forms) with no step count or progress indicator.

topic: Motivation and memory of the experience
text: Peak-End Rule (Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber & Redelmeier, "When More Pain Is Preferred to Less: Adding a Better End", 1993): the strongest moment and the closing moment of a journey get deliberate design, because they shape how the whole is remembered and bad moments stick harder than good ones.
check: walk the journey's end states (confirmation, success, error, cancellation, waiting for a result) — (disposable only) reach success and confirmation for real; read-only: fake them with `page.route` and `route.fulfill()`, or read their templates; a bare or confusing ending, or an unmitigated negative peak (long unexplained wait, harsh error) breaks it.

text: Jakob's Law (Jakob Nielsen, NN/g): the product follows the conventions users learned elsewhere; a redesign lets people stay on the old version for a transition period.
check: compare conventions against common products of the same kind (logo links home, cart top-right, search field looks like a field, standard control behaviour); where the repo or release notes show a major redesign, no preview or opt-out period for it.

text: Postel's Law, robustness principle (Jon Postel, TCP specification): the product is strict in its own output and tolerant of what users type — it normalises any input whose meaning is clear, states the limits it enforces, and says plainly what it did with the value.
check: enter phone numbers with spaces/dashes/+country, card numbers with spaces, dates in several formats, emails with trailing spaces or capitals, pasted values; any rejection where meaning is clear breaks it. Grep for strict regex validation on such fields without normalisation.

text: Paradox of the Active User (Rosson & Carroll, 1987): people dive in without reading instructions, so help lives where they are working (tooltips, inline hints), whichever route they took.
check: help available only in separate docs, up-front tutorials or skippable carousels; features with no in-context explanation where first-time users stall.

text: Proximity, common region and uniform connectedness (Gestalt laws of grouping): things that belong together sit nearer each other than to anything else, share a container (border or background fill), or are joined by a line or frame, so the structure reads at a glance.
check: label-to-field spacing per VIS-17; equal spacing within and between groups; related controls split across regions; a group's members not enclosed or connected. Spacing scales: see visual.md.

text: Similarity (Gestalt laws of grouping): elements that do the same thing look the same, elements that do different things look different, and links and navigation never look like plain text.
check: links styled as body text; clickable and non-clickable cards/chips that look identical; same action styled differently across screens.

text: Aesthetic-Usability Effect (Kurosu & Kashimura, Hitachi Design Center, 1995; 26 ATM UI variants, 252 participants): good looks raise how usable people think a product is and make them forgive small flaws, which can hide real problems in testing — so a verdict rests on observed behaviour, not on opinions.
check: on the most polished screens, count task failures, errors and time from traces; failures there are findings even when testers (human or agent) praise the look, and praise alone is never evidence.

text: Size every touch target to its platform's recommended size: 44×44 pt for iOS/iPadOS (Apple's default; under Apple's 28×28 pt minimum fails, 28-43 pt is a weaker finding), 48×48 dp for Android, 7.5 mm for Windows touch, and 24×24 CSS px on the web (AA) or 44×44 for AAA.
check: measure `boundingBox()` in Playwright for each `a, button, input, select, [role=button], [onclick]` (see Measure); run Android Accessibility Scanner or Xcode Accessibility Inspector; lay a 44 pt grid over a screenshot.

text: On the web, a target smaller than 24×24 CSS px fails unless it passes the 24 px circle test, sits inside running text, is untouched browser UI, has a size that is essential or legally required, or another compliant control on the page does the same job. A11Y-40 is the WCAG line; this rule is its detail.
check: centre a 24 px circle on each small target's bounding box and look for overlap with neighbours; rows of 16 px tall buttons stacked directly on each other fail.

text: Enlarge the touchable region, not necessarily the drawing: add padding around small icons until the hit area meets TOUCH-1's size, leaving the visual size alone.
check: Android Views — `paddingLeft + minWidth + paddingRight ≥ 48dp`, same sum vertically; Compose — a custom `clickable` lacking `sizeIn(minWidth = 48.dp, minHeight = 48.dp)` or `minimumInteractiveComponentSize()`; web — an icon button whose `width/height` is under 24px with zero padding.

text: Leave room between neighbouring targets: 8 dp or more on Android; around 12 pt (bezeled) or 24 pt (no bezel) of padding on Apple platforms.
check: measure the gap between adjacent targets from a screenshot or layout bounds; icon toolbars and the trailing icons of list rows fail most often.

text: Give high-stakes targets more size and more padding, and move them away from the content edge and from controls people hit often.
check: Delete/Pay/Send flush against a frequently tapped control; a tiny dismiss "x" next to a Follow or Buy button.

text: In Compose, give each small clickable its own 48 dp minimum; otherwise the automatic hit-area expansion can spill into a neighbour's touch area.
check: a `.clickable` composable smaller than 48.dp placed next to another clickable.

text: Keep standard gestures on their standard jobs: tap to activate or select, swipe to reveal actions, dismiss or scroll, drag to move, touch-and-hold for extra options, pinch to zoom. A well-known gesture must not trigger something unique to the app, and a standard action must not need a new gesture.
check: grep custom recognizers (`UISwipeGestureRecognizer`, `UILongPressGestureRecognizer`, `pointerInput`, `detectTapGestures`, `GestureDetector`, Hammer.js, `touchstart`) and compare each action against that list.

text: Back every gesture with a visible control; the gesture only speeds things up. Apple's examples: a Back button alongside edge-swipe back, a button alongside swipe-to-dismiss.
check: for each gesture handler, look for a button or menu item that does the same; if there is none, report it.

text: Anything driven by a multipoint gesture (pinch, two fingers) or a path-based one (tracing a route or pattern) also works with one pointer and plain taps, unless the path itself is essential (WCAG 2.5.1, A).
check: a map, carousel or image viewer that offers only pinch or swipe, with no +/- or previous/next buttons.

text: Anything done by dragging can also be done by one pointer without dragging (WCAG 2.5.7, AA): sortable lists, sliders, kanban cards, map panning inside custom scroll areas.
check: grep `draggable`, `dragstart`, `react-beautiful-dnd`, `dnd-kit`, `SortableJS`, `onDragGesture`, `.draggable(`; confirm a tap-then-tap-destination path, up/down buttons or a menu. Native browser scrolling is out of scope; scrolling the page reimplements is in scope.

text: Complete actions on release, and let people back out (slide off before lifting) or undo; acting on touch-down is only acceptable when that is essential (WCAG 2.5.2, A).
check: grep `touchstart`, `pointerdown`, `mousedown`, `onPressIn`, `ACTION_DOWN` handlers that navigate, submit, delete or buy.

text: Any feature triggered by shaking, tilting or other movement also needs an on-screen control, plus a way to switch motion triggering off (WCAG 2.5.4, A).
check: grep `devicemotion`, `deviceorientation`, `CMMotionManager`, `motionEnded`, `SensorManager`, `TYPE_ACCELEROMETER`; find the equivalent button and the off setting.

text: Leave system edge gestures to the system. On Android an inward swipe from the left or right edge means Back and the bottom edge belongs to Home and app switching, which apps cannot override; carve out edge regions with `setSystemGestureExclusionRects` only where truly needed, and in games only while playing. On Apple platforms, avoid custom gestures that clash with system ones.
check: carousels or drawers whose swipe starts at the screen edge; `setSystemGestureExclusionRects` calls with large or always-on rects; custom edge-pan recognizers on iOS.

text: A custom gesture (touch-and-hold included) has to be findable, easy to do, unlike other gestures, and taught inside the app.
check: a feature reachable only through long-press, double-tap or multi-finger gestures, with no hint, menu entry or onboarding.

text: When a gesture cannot work, say so visibly instead of doing nothing (an item that is locked and won't drag, a disabled button that still looks active).
check: try the gesture on locked or disabled items in the running app; no visible response means a finding.

text: Respond during the gesture, not after: the item tracks the finger and the swipe exposes the action progressively, so people can see what will happen and how far to go.
check: record a swipe or drag; if nothing moves until the finger lifts, report it.

text: Reserve row swipes for the destructive actions people look for there; every swipe-delete needs a confirmation or an undo that is easy to spot; important actions must also be reachable without swiping.
check: swipe a list row partway to reveal its actions; (disposable only) complete a swipe-delete — read-only: read its handler for undo or confirmation; deletion with no undo snackbar/toast and no confirmation is a finding, as is an action available only behind the swipe.

text: Keep pinch zoom working: the viewport tag follows WEB-53 (iOS 10 and later disregards `maximum-scale` by default, other browsers may honour it), and no `touch-action: none` sits on page-wide containers.
check: the viewport grep in WEB-53; `touch-action: none` on `html`, `body` or full-page wrappers.

text: Expect many grips, swapped frequently: across 1,333 observations (780 people touching the screen) Hoober saw 49% one-handed, 36% cradled and 15% two-handed use, with people changing grip within seconds.
check: a flow usable only with two hands (a frequent action needs reaches to opposite far corners) or only in one orientation.

text: Place primary content and actions mid-screen, secondary actions on the top and bottom edges, and tertiary functions in menus; Hoober's later data shows the centre is touched most, fastest and most accurately, and people prefer it. His 2013 thumb-zone drawings were withdrawn by him, so do not base findings on them.
check: a primary action in a top corner; any finding that leans on a green/yellow/red thumb-zone overlay.

text: Make edge and corner targets bigger than central ones: in Hoober's data, 95% of taps landed within 7 mm at the centre and about 12 mm at the corners.
check: corner icons (close, back, overflow) built at no more than the platform minimum.

text: Separate risky or unrelated controls from frequent ones, and keep them out of the upper-left area that a right thumb struggles to reach one-handed.
check: a destructive action next to a frequent one, or sitting in the top-left corner.

text: For a handful of top-level destinations use a persistent bottom tab bar (beyond 5 they stop fitting); a hamburger menu hides options more than any other pattern, so it must not be the only navigation.
check: count the top-level destinations; report navigation that exists only inside a menu icon with no visible tabs.

text: Adjust layout to the input: under `@media (pointer: coarse)` (the main pointer is imprecise, such as a finger) give targets more room, and use `any-pointer` when any attached pointer matters, not just the main one.
check: grep CSS for `pointer: coarse` / `any-pointer`; a compact desktop layout sent unchanged to touch devices.

text: Hover reveals need a tap path: WEB-57 owns the rule. On touch, `hover: none` matches devices whose main input cannot hover, or can only fake it through a long press.
check: grep `:hover` rules that toggle `display`/`visibility`/`opacity` of menus or buttons, and `mouseenter`/`mouseover` handlers lacking a click/tap equivalent; in Playwright with `hasTouch`, try opening the menu with `tap()` alone.

text: Include `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width">`: the page gets a mobile layout and loses the old 300-350 ms tap delay (removed for such pages from Chrome 32 on); `touch-action: manipulation` drops double-tap zoom and its click delay while leaving pinch zoom intact.
check: no viewport meta, or a fixed-width one; lag between tap and response in a trace.

text: Give every custom button and tappable row a visible pressed state (`:active` or similar), so the tap registers visually before the result lands.
check: custom `div`/`span` click targets with no `:active` style plus `-webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent`; a mid-tap screenshot that looks identical to the resting state.

text: Never rely on `navigator.vibrate`: MDN lists it as limited availability (not Baseline); Safari and iOS Safari lack it, desktop Firefox dropped it in 129, Firefox for Android returns `true` but never vibrates, and Chrome for Android needs a user gesture (from 60) and refuses it in cross-origin iframes (from 55).
check: grep `navigator.vibrate`; any message or confirmation delivered by vibration alone.

text: Haptics reinforce what the screen and sound already say; they never carry information on their own, and the app stays fully usable with them switched off.
check: an outcome (success, error, limit hit) whose handler fires a haptic but changes nothing visible or audible.

text: Offer a way to disable haptics and obey the system. On Android, `performHapticFeedback` and the other haptic APIs follow the user's touch-feedback setting; on iOS the Taptic Engine stays silent in Low Power Mode, when switched off in Settings, and while the camera or dictation runs.
check: UI feedback routed through paths that skip settings (Android `Vibrator.vibrate`); a haptics-heavy app or game with no in-app switch.

text: Pick system haptics by what they are documented to mean: iOS `UIFeedbackGenerator` offers Notification (a task's result, as success, warning or error, so those three outcomes never share one pattern), Impact (a physical bump, such as something snapping into place) and Selection (a value stepping through choices); on Android reach for `HapticFeedbackConstants` (`CONFIRM`, `REJECT`, `VIRTUAL_KEY` and others) before building custom effects. Do not borrow a pattern for some other meaning.
check: grep the calls (see Measure) and match each to its trigger; an error playing a success notification, success, warning and error sharing one pattern, or a selection tick on a plain button press are findings.

text: One interaction, one haptic, across the whole app, and the same haptic the system uses for well-known controls such as pickers and keyboards.
check: list every haptic call with its trigger; similar actions with different or absent haptics are findings.

text: Use haptics sparingly: short pulses for discrete events, barely perceptible ones for very frequent events (scrolling, dragging a text handle), stronger ones for important events than for routine ones.
check: a haptic inside a scroll or `onChange` handler that fires every frame; heavy impacts on everyday taps; long continuous haptics outside games.

text: Choose crisp haptics over buzzy, ringing ones, and for touch feedback prefer no haptic at all to a buzzy one. Do not use legacy one-shot vibrations (`VibrationEffect.createOneShot`, `Vibrator.vibrate(long)`, `Vibrator.vibrate(long[], int)`) for feedback: a keyclick should take 10-20 ms, yet the actuator can keep ringing for another 20-50 ms.
check: grep `createOneShot`, `createWaveform`, `vibrate(` on UI taps; Flutter `HapticFeedback.vibrate()` used for routine feedback.

text: Time each haptic to land with its animation and sound; a mismatch makes the device feel faulty.
check: a haptic that fires after an `await` or network call when the animation already finished, or before the animation begins.

text: Hold haptics back while the camera, gyroscope or microphone is working.
check: haptic calls inside capture, recording or motion-tracking flows.

text: The pencil or stylus must work on every control, and touching the canvas with it must draw at once, without first picking a mode or pressing a button.
check: controls that respond to a finger but ignore pencil/stylus input (Android: handlers that discard `TOOL_TYPE_STYLUS` pointers); a "draw mode" switch needed before inking.

text: Pencil hover may preview but never act, Apple Pencil double-tap must not run anything destructive, and the user's system-wide double-tap choice should be honoured.
check: hover handlers that commit changes; double-tap wired to delete or clear.

text: Remove strokes the system later cancels: on Android, after `ACTION_CANCEL` (navigation gesture, palm rejection) or `FLAG_CANCELED` (Android 13+), drop that pointer's stroke since its last `ACTION_DOWN` and redraw.
check: grep the drawing surface's touch handler for `ACTION_CANCEL` and `FLAG_CANCELED`; a resting palm that leaves marks is a finding.

text: Place drawing-app controls so neither a left nor a right hand covers them, or make them movable.
check: a fixed palette on one side that the drawing hand hides.

text: How a haptic feels is judged in its final context, on a physical device that supports haptics, not from the code or on a desktop. Which pattern each meaning gets is TOUCH-31's, one haptic per interaction is TOUCH-32's, and agreeing with screen and sound is TOUCH-29's.
check: on a supported device, play each call on the TOUCH-32 list through read-only actions ((disposable only) for one behind a write; read-only: leave it to the code review of TOUCH-29 to TOUCH-36); two meanings that feel alike in the hand though the code gives them different patterns, or a haptic felt where no call was found (a library or system default firing).

text: Some Apple devices have no haptics at all (iPad, iPod touch, Apple Vision Pro): check `CHHapticEngine.capabilitiesForHardware().supportsHaptics` and give those devices the same information as sound or a visual cue.
check: read the code paths: a confirmation that exists only as a haptic, so iPad users get nothing; Core Haptics code with no `supportsHaptics` branch.

text: Size web body copy between 15-25 px (Butterick); USWDS puts the floor at an effective 16 px, with smaller text kept for captions and footnotes.
check: computed `font-size` on `p`/body copy in DevTools; grep CSS for paragraph/body `font-size` under `16px`/`1rem`.

text: Hold body text to 45-90 characters per line, spaces counted; aim near 66 for long reading. WCAG 1.4.8 (AAA) sets 80 as the ceiling (40 CJK).
check: text containers lacking a `max-width` (e.g. `max-width: 66ch`); count characters per line in a 1440 px-wide screenshot — paragraphs spanning the full desktop width fail.

text: Give body text leading of 120-145% of its size (Butterick); USWDS wants 1.5 or more for long passages and 1-1.35 for headings and short bits.
check: computed `line-height` on paragraphs; multi-line text at `line-height: 1`, `normal`, or a px value equal to the font size fails.

text: Space paragraphs further apart than their lines (1.4.8: at least 1.5× the line spacing), and put at least 1.5× more space above a heading than below it, so it reads as the start of the next section.
check: compare `margin-top` with `margin-bottom` on `h1`-`h6`; a bottom margin equal to or bigger than the top one fails.

text: Align running text to the left on the web; if a block must be justified, switch hyphenation on with it.
check: grep for `text-align: justify` with no `hyphens: auto` on the same element; look for rivers and wide word gaps in screenshots.

text: Limit capitals-only text to under a line (labels, short headings, captions) and track it out by 5-12%; for emphasising a passage use weight, size or a rule instead of capitals.
check: grep `text-transform: uppercase` and see what it styles — paragraphs, body or alert text fail; uppercase without any `letter-spacing` is a weaker finding.

text: Let only links carry an underline; use bold or italic for emphasis.
check: grep `text-decoration: underline` / `<u>` applied to anything that is not a link.

text: Work with at most 3 type sizes for the body/subheader/header levels of a view; the most important thing gets the largest size, and no more than 2 elements are large.
check: tally distinct `font-size` values per screen from computed styles and across the repo (`grep -ohE 'font-size:\s*[^;]+' -r src | sort | uniq -c`); many one-off sizes outside the scale fail.

text: Take text sizes from a defined type scale (e.g. M3 baseline: Body Large 16sp, Body Medium 14sp, Body Small 12sp, Label Small 11sp), not ad-hoc values, so hierarchy and user text scaling hold together.
check: literal font sizes in components where scale tokens or text styles (`textAppearance*`, `MaterialTheme.typography`, CSS custom properties) should be.

text: Keep typefaces few, and stay off Ultralight, Thin and Light weights at small sizes.
check: count distinct `font-family` values and `@font-face` families; grep `font-weight: 100|200|300` on text below ~16 px.

text: Give each colour a single job: the colour that signals interactivity never dresses static text, and status colours are not spent on decoration.
check: locate the link/accent token and grep for it on headings, labels or icons that have no handler.

text: Choose colours by role rather than appearance: pair every container colour with its matching on-colour (M3 `colorPrimary`/`colorOnPrimary`, `colorError`/`colorOnError`, `colorSurface`/`colorOnSurface`), and use error colours only for errors.
check: `onSurface` text sitting on a `primary` fill, or a token picked only because its value matched — these break once the theme changes.

text: Define a light, a dark and a higher-contrast version of each custom colour.
check: custom colours with a single value and no dark counterpart (no `values-night`, no `prefers-color-scheme: dark` override, no Color Set appearance variants).

text: Colour is never the only cue: A11Y-12 owns the rule; in visual design the usual misses are listed in this Check.
check: status dots/pills, red/green deltas or chart series that carry no label or icon.

text: Allow for colours meaning different things in different markets (e.g. red signals a rise in Chinese Stocks).
check: localised builds that hard-wire red/green to down/up.

text: Draw every margin, padding and gap from a single spacing scale (Carbon: 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 80, 96, 160 px; Android: steps of 8 dp, with 4 dp for small elements).
check: `grep -ohE '(margin|padding|gap)[^:]*:\s*[^;]+' -r src | sort | uniq -c`; off-scale values (5px, 13px, 18px...) show drift.

text: Put things that belong together closer than things that don't; a label should be nearer its own field than the field before it.
check: in a screenshot, compare the gap from a label to its field with the gap from that field to the next label; equal or reversed gaps fail.

text: Line elements up on shared edges, and indent only what is subordinate.
check: overlay left edges on a screenshot; ragged starts inside one column, or indented items that are not children, fail.

text: Order content by importance, starting at the top and leading edge.
check: the main task sits below secondary panels in the first viewport.

text: Keep content that matters away from spots and styles people associate with ads (top banner, right rail, boxed or animated promo look), because users skip those.
check: key notices or CTAs shown as banners, side-rail cards or with ad-style animation; confirm with a usability test.

text: Give images and surfaces a consistent aspect ratio (Android recommends 16:9, 3:2, 4:3, 1:1, 3:4, 2:3) and reserve their space — layout shift is in web.md.
check: mixed ratios in one image grid; `` with neither `width`/`height` nor `aspect-ratio`.

text: Allow a single primary button or CTA within each page or region.
check: count primary/filled button variants per view (`variant="primary"`, `.btn-primary`, `Button appearance="primary"`); two or more in one container fail.

text: Greyed-out buttons that hide why: WEB-22 owns the rule for forms; any other disabled button says nearby what would enable it.
check: `disabled` buttons with no visible reason; submit buttons: WEB-22's Check.

text: Ration emphasis; when every element is bright or high-contrast, none of them leads. The law is LAW-10; the button count is VIS-22.
check: per region, find the lead element; any other element with the same colour, size and weight as the lead fails.

text: Mark links with a colour distinct from body text and use that same style everywhere; adding an underline to the colour makes clickability most obvious. Show visited links in a duller tone than unvisited ones.
check: inline links coloured like body text, link styles that differ between pages, no `:visited` rule.

text: Make controls read as clickable through shape and edge even in a flat style, and never give headings or static text the look of a button or link.
check: buttons that are bare text with no border or fill; headings on coloured backgrounds; `cursor: pointer` on elements with no handler; clickable `div`s that look like plain text.

text: Use strong signifiers on dense or unusual layouts — in NN/g's study, weak ones cost 22% more time and 25% more fixations.
check: ghost or flat controls on content-heavy pages; first-time users hesitating in a first-contact run.

text: Put a visible text label beside icons, apart from the handful almost everyone recognises (home, print, search); a hover tooltip is not a label.
check: icon-only toolbar/navigation buttons (`<button><svg/></button>` with only `title`/`aria-label`); the accessible name is A11Y's concern, the visible label is this rule's.

text: Bind each icon to one function product-wide, and take icons from one set.
check: one glyph used for different actions; several icon libraries in use (`grep -r "from 'lucide\|heroicons\|@mui/icons\|fontawesome"`).

text: Check icons by asking users what they think each one does; when no fitting icon comes to mind within 5 seconds, use a word.
check: abstract or custom glyphs without labels on non-standard actions.

text: Add motion only when it explains something; skip it on interactions people repeat often, and let users act before an animation finishes.
check: decorative entrances on every list item; input locked during transitions (`pointer-events: none` until `animationend`).

text: Keep UI animations between 100-500 ms: around 100 ms for small feedback like toggles and checkboxes, 200-300 ms for big changes such as modals; at 500 ms they start to feel sluggish. Make exits a little quicker than entrances. NN/g and M3 differ on large moves: M3 lets duration grow with the area covered (VIS-33).
check: grep `transition-duration`, `animation-duration`, `duration:` values; ≥ 500 ms on small, frequent feedback (toggles, checkboxes, menus, tooltips, list items) fails; full-screen or shared-element transitions may use VIS-33's long tokens.

text: Take durations from tokens, not literals — M3: short 50-200 ms, medium 250-400 ms, long 450-600 ms, extra-long 700-1000 ms; Carbon: 70, 110, 150, 240, 400, 700 ms — and lengthen them as the distance or area covered grows: long and extra-long are for large-area moves only, and VIS-32's ceiling holds for small feedback.
check: count distinct duration literals in CSS/JS; many one-offs, or long durations on small elements, fail.

text: Ease in-coming elements with a decelerating curve, out-going ones with an accelerating curve, and on-screen moves with the standard curve (M3 standard `cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1)`, decelerate `(0, 0, 0, 1)`, accelerate `(0.3, 0, 1, 1)`; Carbon productive standard `(0.2, 0, 0.38, 0.9)`); use Carbon's productive style for task UI and expressive for significant moments.
check: `linear` on UI movement, `ease-in` on entrances.

text: Respect the reduced-motion setting by dropping or swapping scale, pan and parallax effects, and never let motion be the sole carrier of information.
check: grep for `prefers-reduced-motion` (CSS/JS), `UIAccessibility.isReduceMotionEnabled`, `ANIMATOR_DURATION_SCALE`; absent while large-motion animation exists fails. Platform detail: WEB-58 (web), IOS-49 (Apple).

text: Follow the system light/dark choice by default; a hard-locked appearance is a finding everywhere. An in-app override splits by platform: Apple discourages it (IOS-37), Android and Windows expect a Light/Dark/System picker (AND-40, DESK-55). Outside Apple platforms, the web included, a picker that defaults to System passes.
check: a locked mode fails; `overrideUserInterfaceStyle`, hard-set `AppCompatDelegate.MODE_NIGHT_NO/YES`, CSS with neither `prefers-color-scheme` nor `color-scheme`.

text: Base dark themes on dark grey rather than pure black, and convey elevation with progressively lighter tonal surfaces, because shadows hardly register on dark backgrounds.
check: `#000`/`black` as page or surface background in dark theme; dark-theme cards separated only by `box-shadow`.

text: In dark mode hold text contrast at 4.5:1 or better and target 7:1 for custom colours, small text especially (Apple); re-check with Increase Contrast and Reduce Transparency switched on.
check: contrast tool on dark-theme screenshots — thresholds as in A11Y-14.

text: Review every screen, image and icon in both appearances; tone down images with white backgrounds and give icons that disappear on dark an outline.
check: screenshot each route in light and dark; logos or illustrations showing white boxes or losing detail on dark.

text: Use semantic colours that adapt to the appearance instead of fixed colour values.
check: `grep -rnE '#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}\b|rgba?\(' src` outside the token/theme file; `Color(red:...)`, `UIColor(red:`, `Color(0xFF...)` in views.

text: Define colour, type, spacing and motion as design tokens selected by meaning, so a theme, dark mode or a brand change lands everywhere at once.
check: share of literal values versus token references in styles; appearance-named tokens (`blue-500`) used straight in components where role tokens (`color.text.danger`) belong.

text: Style every element of a given type the same way (one link style; one style per button variant).
check: compare computed styles of all `a` and each `button` variant across pages; near-duplicate component implementations.

text: Right-align quantities that add up (amounts, percentages, currency, tallies) and set them in tabular or monospace figures; phone numbers, ZIP codes and dates need neither.
check: numeric `td` lacking `text-align: right`; no `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`.

text: Use one unit and format per column, give every table a header row, and pin header rows/columns when the table outgrows the screen.
check: mixed units within a column; no `thead`; long tables without `position: sticky` headers.

text: Label chart series in place rather than through a legend when the labels fit; leave the legend off for a single series; add texture or labels so no series depends on colour.
check: multi-series charts identified only by a colour legend.

topic: Iconography: the right icon for the job
text: For a well-known action, use the icon people already know for it, drawn the way the platform draws it: trash for delete, pencil for edit, gear for settings, magnifier for search, the platform's own share symbol. Before drawing a new icon, look at what competitors and the target platform use. A familiar icon never takes on a different meaning (a hamburger that means "list", a trash can that archives): even a slight shift costs the icon its trust.
check: set each icon crop from `reveal.js` beside the action it performs; a familiar action with an unfamiliar icon, or a familiar icon on a different action.

topic: Iconography: the right icon for the job
text: Icons whose meanings compete — heart, star, bookmark, flag — get one fixed meaning across the product and a visible label. An icon nobody recognises hides its feature as well as a menu does. Draw icons simple and schematic, so they still read at their smallest size.
check: the icon test's wrong answers; two of heart, star and bookmark in one product for different jobs; detailed icons that blur at 16–24 px.

text: Acknowledge every action quickly and visibly. Under 0.1 s a response reads as instant, up to 1 s the user's train of thought survives, and beyond 10 s attention drifts to something else. This rule owns the pass/fail line for response time: no visible change by 1 s is a finding; on the web, INP over 200 ms (WEB-50) is the field metric for the same thing; the Doherty 0.4 s (LAW-1) is a target, not a fail line.
check: time each control on a slow network (SKILL.md: Slow network) with a screen recording or trace (web: the DevTools Performance panel); a wait over 1 s with nothing changing on screen is a finding.

text: Match the indicator to the wait: nothing below 1 s; from about 1 s some progress cue, and since the sources name no type for 1-2 s, a busy state on the control is enough; an indeterminate spinner for 2 to 10 s on a control or region (for a whole page or view, the skeleton of WEB-60); and at 10 s or more a percent-done bar with a cancel option. This rule owns the timings; WEB-60 owns which loader fits what is loading.
check: on a slow network (SKILL.md: Slow network), look for spinners that blink on quick loads, spinners on uploads/exports, and long jobs that cannot be stopped.

text: Name things the way the audience does, using their domain vocabulary rather than the product's internals.
check: grep UI strings for DB column names, enum constants, HTTP status codes and internal codenames.

text: Stick to the conventions of the wider web and use one term and one control per concept throughout; visitors arrive trained by other sites (Jakob's law).
check: collect the terms and controls used for a single concept (the verbs for one action, such as "Delete"/"Remove": TEXT-55 owns them); a logo that does not go home; links that do not look clickable.

text: Keep choices on screen so people can pick instead of remember, and never make them memorise something from one screen to type on another.
check: a code or ID displayed on an earlier step and asked for later; menus made only of unlabelled icons.

text: Every flow, dialog and mode needs an obvious way out, and actions people may regret need a way back.
check: modals lacking a close or Cancel; multi-step flows lacking Back. Destructive actions with no undo, restore or fitting confirmation: WEB-68 owns them.

text: Reach for undo before a confirmation; ask for confirmation only when the result is severe or permanent, never for everyday actions. A confirmation names what will happen, its buttons name the outcomes ("Delete file"/"Keep file"), and the destructive choice is not preselected.
check: grep `confirm(` and "Are you sure"; Yes/No/OK buttons; autofocus on the destructive button; confirmations on save, archive or favourite.

text: The browser Back button must lead to the prior page exactly as the user left it.
check: press Back inside SPA flows; wiped form state, missing history entries or being thrown out of the app is a finding.

text: Reserve modals for critical warnings or input the current task cannot proceed without; promotional or off-task content never goes in a modal, and nothing modal interrupts checkout.
check: newsletter or promo modals on load or during checkout.

text: Errors never go in toasts or notifications that vanish on a timer; attach them to the input at fault. Success feedback appears next to the control that caused it.
check: grep toast/snackbar calls inside error/catch paths; an "Added to cart" banner far from its button.

text: Anything needed to finish the task (instructions, format rules) sits on the page, not in a tooltip; tooltips stay short and add something the visible label does not already say.
check: `title=` or tooltip text carrying format rules or required info; tooltips that echo the button text.

text: Tooltips open on keyboard focus too, not only on hover, and touch screens get a tap target (an "i" popup) instead.
check: tooltip handlers bound only to `mouseenter`.

text: Every question must earn its place: record why it is asked and what the answer is used for, and remove the rest. Baymard: most checkouts need only 8 fields; the 2024 average was 11.3.
check: count fields per form; flag any whose answer nothing downstream uses.

text: Break long forms up using the "one thing per page" pattern (a single question, decision or fact per screen), and route people past questions that do not apply to them.
check: long single-page forms; questions everyone sees that only a few need.

text: Stack form fields in one column; only parts of a single value (date parts, card expiry and CVC) may sit side by side.
check: desktop-width screenshot showing unrelated fields on one row.

text: Each input carries a label that stays visible, placed above the field on mobile; placeholder text is never the label, hint or example.
check: `<input placeholder=` with no `<label>`; labels that live inside the field.

text: Flag required and optional fields both, each at the label (an asterisk, and the word "Optional"); a single notice like "All fields are required" is not enough. (GOV.UK takes the opposite line and rules out asterisks for mandatory fields.)
check: forms flagging only one kind of field, or neither.

text: Put `autocomplete` tokens on personal, address, payment and password inputs (`email`, `postal-code`, `cc-number`, `cc-exp`, `current-password`, `new-password`, `one-time-code`), and take card and phone numbers in a single input each.
check: grep inputs with no `autocomplete`; phone or card numbers split across boxes.

text: Summon the right on-screen keyboard with `inputmode` (`numeric`, `decimal`, `tel`, `email`, `url`, `search`) rather than `type="number"` for codes and integers, and set `enterkeyhint` (`next`, `done`, `go`, `search`, `send`) to label the Enter key with its real effect.
check: grep `type="number"` on card, postcode, account or OTP fields; search and chat inputs lacking `enterkeyhint`.

text: Let people type card numbers with spaces and group the digits as they type (4-4-4-4; Amex 4-6-5); do not reject, strip or length-cap the input.
check: enter a card number containing spaces; an error or silent stripping is a finding.

text: When a form comes back with errors, every value the user typed is still there, card details included.
check: (disposable only) submit with one bad field; any emptied field is a finding. Read-only: in the guarded session the guard's 503 is a failed submit too, and every field must survive it (the 503 is not the finding; an emptied field is).

text: Leave submit buttons enabled and explain problems after the attempt instead. Where duplicate submissions really occur, drop the repeat click and show that work is in progress.
check: submit `disabled` until the form is valid; (disposable only) a double click creating two records — read-only: double-click in the guarded session and count the writes it logs to `blocked.txt`.

text: The main button's label is in sentence case and names what it does ("Continue", rather than "Next" or "Submit"). How many primary buttons: VIS-22.
check: vague labels on primary buttons.

text: Multi-step transactions end with a summary of answers before the final submit; each Change link brings the user back to that summary once edited.
check: no summary step; a Change link that replays the whole flow.

text: Checkout always works without an account, and the offer to create one waits until after the order is placed.
check: an account wall before payment; a "Create account" step inside checkout.

text: Do not flag a field while the person is still typing it; check it when focus leaves (Baymard) or when the form is submitted (GOV.UK). Once a message is showing, remove it on the keystroke that makes the value correct.
check: type into an email field; an error after the first character, or one that stays after the fix.

text: After a failed submit, place an error summary at the top of `main` with the heading "There is a problem", send focus there, make each entry a link to its field, start the `<title>` with "Error: ", and show identical wording beside each faulty field.
check: submit an empty form in the guarded session, where client-side validation answers before any write; (disposable only) for the server's own errors — read-only: fake its 400/422 with `page.route` and `route.fulfill()`. Inspect focus, title, links and whether the wording matches.

text: An error message names the problem and the fix in everyday words ("Enter your first name", "Name must be 35 characters or less"). It is never an error code, and avoids "valid", "invalid", "forbidden", "illegal", "you forgot", "oops", "please" and "sorry".
check: grep for "An error occurred", "Invalid", "This field is required", raw exception text and the words above.

text: Design mistakes out: restrict inputs to what is possible, suggest probable corrections, and warn before a likely slip such as a mentioned but missing attachment.
check: free text where a picker would do; no "did you mean" suggestion on emails or addresses.

text: Desktop layouts show top-level navigation openly along the top or left, not in a hamburger (people used hidden menus in 27% of desktop cases, against 48 to 50% for visible ones). Mobile shows up to 4 top links openly; if more must be hidden, key destinations are also linked from the page body.
check: screenshots at ≥1024 px and 375 px where a hamburger is the only navigation.

text: Link wording: TEXT-26 owns the rule; menu items too must let people guess where they go, so in-house jargon in navigation fails.
check: read the navigation labels; product codenames or internal team names fail; link text: TEXT-26's Check.

text: Sort long menus by how often items are used and put controls used in sequence next to each other: more options slow the choice (Hick's law), and farther, smaller targets slow the pointer (Fitts's law).
check: long menus in arbitrary order; a submit button far from the last field.

text: Lead with what matters (key points early: TEXT-21): headings and link text that start with their most telling words, and text broken up by subheadings, lists and bolded key terms (readers skim in an F-pattern).
check: headings beginning "Welcome to" or "Introduction"; unbroken blocks of prose.

text: Search is a text field visible at the top of the page, not a link or bare icon, and is wide enough to show a typical query.
check: a desktop homepage whose search hides behind an icon; a box too narrow for common queries.

text: A search with no hits still offers a way forward: the query stays visible, alongside simpler or alternative queries (each previewing its top 3 to 5 results), related categories and links to support.
check: search for gibberish and for a typo; a page that only says "No results" is a finding.

text: Autocomplete lists hold ≤10 suggestions on desktop and 4 to 8 on mobile; Up/Down move through them and Enter picks one; emphasis goes on the suggested completion rather than the letters already typed.
check: type a single letter, count suggestions, and arrow through them.

text: Active filters are listed together, each removable on its own (an "x") with a Clear all as well; a bare count of active filters is not enough.
check: apply 2 filters and try to drop one without reopening the filter panel.

text: No region is ever just blank: an empty state explains the cause (nothing yet, filters, still loading) and offers the action that would fill it.
check: screenshots of a fresh account ((disposable only) to create one — read-only: fake an empty list with `page.route` and `route.fulfill()`, or read the empty-state code) and of over-filtered lists; "No records" appearing before the data arrives on a slow network (SKILL.md: Slow network).

text: Losing the connection is announced right away, along with what can still be done; cached content stays readable and user actions are queued to sync later rather than blocked.
check: cut the network (SKILL.md: Slow network; web: `context.setOffline(true)` or DevTools "Offline"); a blank screen, an endless spinner or lost input is a finding. (disposable only) Act while offline and reconnect: the queued actions write when they sync.

text: When the system is down, apologise and tell people what will happen next; the worst moment and the last moment shape how the whole visit is remembered (peak-end rule).
check: fake a 500 or a timeout — web: `page.route` ending in `route.fulfill({ status: 500 })`, or a long delay then `route.fallback()`, never `route.continue()`, which bypasses the write guard; native: a mock server, the slow network (SKILL.md: Slow network), or (disposable only) a real failure; a generic "Something went wrong" with no next step is a finding.

text: Skip the up-front tutorial carousel where possible; if one exists, keep it short with a prominent Skip, and prefer hints shown at the moment a feature is used.
check: a first-visit carousel that cannot be skipped.

text: Ask for notification, location or camera access only after the user does something that needs it, never as the page loads; a short explainer before the browser prompt is optional.
check: grep `Notification.requestPermission`, `getCurrentPosition`, `getUserMedia` running on load instead of inside a click handler.

text: A refused permission leaves the product usable: read the blocked state through the Permissions API, offer another route (email in place of push, say), and explain how to turn access back on.
check: deny the prompt; a feature that silently breaks is a finding.

text: The first price shown includes shipping, tax and any compulsory fees; nothing is added step by step (drip pricing). Unexpected extra costs are the leading reason shoppers abandon checkout (40%).
check: compare the first price on display with the amount at payment, walking to the payment step and stopping before paying.

text: Cancelling takes no more effort than signing up and works through the same channel, with no retention offers forced in between.
check: count the steps to join and to cancel ((disposable only) by doing both — read-only: walk each flow to its last step without finishing it, and read the routes and help pages); web sign-ups that can only be cancelled by phone.

text: Charge only with the customer's clear, informed agreement: paid extras and subscriptions start unticked, and a free trial states when and at what price it renews.
check: grep `checked` or default-true on paid add-ons and opt-ins; trials with no renewal date or price.

text: Privacy settings are easy to reach and every option gets equal visual weight; defaults collect and share no more than people would anticipate.
check: a consent banner with a bold Accept and a hidden Reject; tracking switched on by default.

text: Urgency, scarcity and popularity claims must be real; a countdown ends when the offer actually ends.
check: reload the page; a timer that restarts or a stock figure that changes at random is a finding.

text: Word every choice even-handedly and respect a refusal: no confirmshaming, misleading wording, ads dressed as content, or prompts that keep coming back after dismissal.
check: read each decline link and opt-out label aloud; dismiss a prompt, move on, and see whether it reappears.

text: Keep LCP ≤ 2.5 s (poor > 4 s), INP ≤ 200 ms (poor > 500 ms), CLS ≤ 0.1 (poor > 0.25), at the 75th percentile of page loads, split mobile/desktop.
check: Lighthouse, PageSpeed Insights or CrUX; the `web-vitals` library for field data.

text: Give images and video `width`/`height` (or `aspect-ratio`), hold space for ads and embeds, and add late content below what is already shown, never above it.
check: grep `<img` lacking width/height; Layout Shift regions in a DevTools Performance recording.

text: Move elements with `transform` rather than `top`/`left`, and tune the fallback font to the web font's metrics (`size-adjust` and the related overrides).
check: grep keyframes and transitions on top/left; text reflowing when fonts arrive.

text: Include `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` and leave zoom enabled: no `user-scalable=no` or `=0`, and no `maximum-scale` under 2 (WCAG's 200% resize); MDN advises allowing 5×.
check: grep the viewport meta tag; `user-scalable=no|0` or `maximum-scale` under 2 fails, under 5 is a weaker finding.

text: Pages fit the viewport width without sideways scrolling; images get `max-width: 100%`; breakpoints follow where the content breaks, not device names.
check: screenshots at 320, 375 and 768 px; `document.documentElement.scrollWidth > innerWidth`.
