text: Use `dvh`/`svh` for full-height layouts instead of `100vh`, which overflows the visible area while mobile browser bars are showing.
check: grep `100vh`; a bottom CTA hidden behind the browser toolbar on a phone.

text: Pages using `viewport-fit=cover` pad their edges with `env(safe-area-inset-*)` so nothing sits under a notch or home indicator.
check: grep `viewport-fit=cover` with no `safe-area-inset`; fixed bottom bars overlapping the home indicator.

text: Nothing is reachable only by hovering; under `@media (hover: none)` or `(pointer: coarse)` every hover reveal has a tap equivalent (target sizes: see touch.md).
check: menus or content revealed only on hover; DevTools touch emulation.

text: The web side of VIS-35: honour `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` by dropping or swapping decorative motion, scaling and panning of large elements first.
check: grep animation code for a `prefers-reduced-motion` branch; emulate it in DevTools Rendering.

text: Under `forced-colors: active`, controls must stay visible: since `box-shadow` and gradient backgrounds are forced to none, draw borders in system colors instead, and do not switch the mode off wholesale with `forced-color-adjust: none`.
check: emulate forced colors in DevTools Rendering; buttons or focus rings that disappear.

text: Size the loader to what is loading: a busy state or small spinner for a local wait (a button, a row, a panel); for a whole page or view, a skeleton whose blocks match the real layout (a bare header and footer frame does not count); one region fetching never blocks the whole screen. WEB-2 owns the timings.
check: load each screen on a slow network (SKILL.md: Slow network); a screen-wide spinner or overlay while one region fetches is a finding; a full-page spinner shown past 2 s where a skeleton would fit is a weaker finding.

text: Show each part as soon as it is ready: frame and primary content first, text before images, offscreen images and heavy assets deferred (web: iframes and scripts too). Reserving space for what arrives late is WEB-51 (images, embeds, ads) and WEB-52 (fonts) on the web; a native app reserves it the same way for late images and embeds, and that native case is checked here.
check: screenshots or a screen recording every second on a slow network (SKILL.md: Slow network); text held back by unrelated assets; native only, content that jumps when an image or embed lands (web: WEB-51, WEB-52).

text: Start work at the first clear signal of intent and acknowledge it at once: a search can fetch on the first keystroke (web: `keydown` rather than `keyup`), an upload can begin when the file is chosen rather than on submit, and a long operation shows its loader the moment it starts.
check: search and lookup handlers that wait for the key to come up (web: bound only to `keyup`) or for submit; uploads that only start on the final button: read-only, read whether the file input's change handler starts the upload; (disposable only) choose a file and watch whether the request leaves before submit.

text: Keep progress honest: a percent-done bar tracks real work and never parks at 99%. When the length is unknown, name the current step and count ("Importing 3 of 12") and phrase estimates loosely ("this can take a few minutes").
check: (disposable only) start a long job on a slow network (SKILL.md: Slow network); a bar that stalls near the end, jumps to done, or a precise estimate that turns out wrong. Read-only: read how the progress value and estimate are computed.

text: Let long jobs run without the user: past about 10 s, offer to continue in the background with a small progress drawer they can walk away from, and say when it is done, in the app or by email.
check: an export, import or report that holds the screen for minutes with no way out, on a slow network (SKILL.md: Slow network) ((disposable only) to start an import — read-only: read the job's UI code for a background path).

text: Refresh without pulling content out from under the reader: data that syncs itself updates quietly; new data for something the user is reading is announced (a banner or toast that loads it on request) rather than reshuffled in.
check: leave a list open while new items arrive (web: serve them with `page.route` and `route.fulfill()`; (disposable only) by creating them); rows that jump or reorder under the cursor.

text: Use optimistic updates for cheap, reversible actions that nearly always succeed (a like, a toggle, add to cart, reordering): show the result at once and confirm in the background. When the server refuses, roll back visibly and say what failed; a silent rollback is a screen that lied. Money, deletes and anything irreversible wait for the server.
check: toggles that wait a round trip before moving: read-only, read whether the handler changes state before the request resolves, or (web) answer the toggle's request with a delayed `page.route` that ends in `route.fulfill()`; (disposable only) flip it on a slow network (SKILL.md: Slow network). On a 500 (web: `page.route` with `route.fulfill({ status: 500 })`; native: a mock server or (disposable only) a real failure), an optimistic change that vanishes without a message.

topic: Finding your way: calm, not hidden
text: Show up front what most users need for most tasks, and nothing that competes with it; put the rest behind a trigger that is plainly visible and labelled so it predicts what is behind it. Go no deeper than two disclosure levels, and give each secondary option one route, not several. A calm screen hides the rare, never the primary.
check: `reveal.js` output: a top-task action behind any revealer or only on hover; anything at depth 3 or more; a trigger labelled only "More", "..." or an icon; one option reachable from several menus.

text: Match the safeguard to the loss: undo for anything that can be reversed; a specific confirmation (WEB-7) for what is permanent; and for the rare, catastrophic ones (deleting an account, a whole project, every record) a step people would never do by habit, such as typing a confirming word. Keep that last tier for the few actions that earn it, or typing becomes the next reflex. A short-lived undo (a snackbar) is backed by somewhere lasting — trash, history, versions — because some regret it days later; and a destructive confirmation looks unlike the routine dialogs, so habit does not click it through.
check: list the destructive controls by hand: filter `reveal.js` output (its controls and its skipped list) by name for delete, remove, erase, clear and close account, since it does not flag them. Read-only: read each one's handler for a confirmation and its wording, an undo, and a soft-delete or trash path. (disposable only) press each and look for the item in trash or history afterwards. Each needs undo, a confirmation naming what is lost, or — for account, project or bulk deletion — a typed confirmation; a typed confirmation on routine deletes is a finding too; so is an undo snackbar with nothing lasting behind it.
